the user is asking why nothing can go faster than the speed of light, using special relativity. let me recall what i know about this.

first, einstein's theory of special relativity, right? it's from 1905. the two main postulates are that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames and that the speed of light in a vacuum is constant for all observers, regardless of their motion relative to the light source.

so, if the speed of light is constant, then as an object moves faster, its mass increases from the perspective of a stationary observer. this is called relativistic mass. the formula for relativistic mass is m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v²/c²), where m0 is the rest mass, v is the velocity, and c is the speed of light. as v approaches c, the denominator approaches zero, making the mass approach infinity. that would require infinite energy to accelerate further, which is impossible. hence, you can't reach or exceed the speed of light.

also, time dilation comes into play. from the observer's frame, time for the moving object slows down. so as you approach the speed of light, time for the object would slow down to a stop at c. but that's more about how time is perceived, not the actual reason why you can't go faster.

another aspect is the relationship between energy and mass. the equation e = mc² shows that mass and energy are interchangeable. as an object's speed increases, its kinetic energy increases, contributing to its mass. again, approaching c would require infinite energy.

there's also the concept of spacetime. in special relativity, as you move through space, you're also moving through time. the faster you go through space, the slower you move through time. but this might not be the primary reason, though it's related to the overall framework.

i should make sure to explain that the speed of light is the ultimate speed limit because of the way the equations work. the math shows that exceeding c would lead to imaginary numbers in the equations, which don't make physical sense. for example, the gamma factor (the denominator in the mass equation) becomes imaginary if v > c, which isn't possible in reality.

also, experiments have confirmed these predictions, like particle accelerators where particles approach the speed of light and require more energy to accelerate further, but never surpass c.

so putting it all together, the reason is the relativistic effects on mass, energy, and time, which make it impossible for any object with mass to reach or exceed the speed of light. the equations of special relativity show that as you approach the speed of light, the energy required becomes infinite, which is unattainable. also, the invariance of the speed of light in all frames of reference means that no matter how fast you're moving, you'll always measure light's speed as c, making it a universal speed limit.
